data.title: Brothers rescue group of elderly people from burning California assisted living facility
data.description:
(KTLA) — Two young brothers worked quickly to rescue a group of elderly people after a fire broke out at an assisted living facility in Glendale, Calif., on Friday.

Glendale firefighters responded to the burning home on the 1800 block of Mountain Street around 4:45 p.m.

As the flames grew and heavy smoke billowed from the home, neighbors Alex Bazinyan, 20, and his brother Narek Bazinyan, 15, realized time was of the essence and decided to run over and help.

“I ran outside and I was looking at the front door when I saw the nurse outside and she was screaming for help,” Alex told Nexstar’s KTLA’s John Fenoglio.

The brothers knew several people were trapped inside the home that was operating as an assisted living facility for seniors.

Narek initially grabbed a garden hose to help quell the flames, but as the blaze grew more intense and screams for help grew louder, they knew they had to run into the fire.

“I go inside this big room and I see all these old people on the floor with catheters,” Alex recalled. “Some people were injured, had blood on their legs. We just took everybody out one by one.”

There were eight people inside the home — two nurses and six elderly residents, most of whom were unable to walk. The brothers said the nurses were desperately trying to remove the elderly residents from the home but were struggling.

“I see a guy in the back about to be engulfed by the flames,” Narek recalled when he entered the home. “The nurse is trying to pick him up. I go and grab his legs and pull him out to the front.”

Soon after, two additional neighbors also ran over to help evacuate the residents.

“As I’m looking around, I just see flames going up and coming towards me,” Narek said. “I tried bringing everyone out as fast as I could. There was smoke everywhere. I was pretty much blinded by the smoke.”

The brothers were able to safely rescue all six elderly residents and placed them on the front lawn as they awaited fire crews.

But just as they moved the last person out of the burning home, Alex recalled hearing a loud explosion. 

“I heard an explosion come from the house,” he said. “I looked back and I didn’t understand what exploded, but I just heard a big boom.”

Firefighters arrived at the home and were able to extinguish the flames before any nearby houses were affected. The Glendale Fire Department chief said an oxygen tank likely exploded, which collapsed part of the home. 

Seven people were transported to the hospital with minor injuries. The cause of the fire remains under investigation.

As for Alex and Narek, they said their instincts just kicked in and the only thing they were focused on was quickly rescuing everyone from the burning home.

“It’s that instinct of whenever you see people in need, you want to help them out,” Alex said. “You don’t really think about who it is. We have a really tight-knit community here.”

Narek agreed, saying, “If you ever see anyone in need, you should always try to help them out as much as you can.”

data.title: Kennedy Center could close as early as Tuesday as officials warn of impending 'fiscal collapse'
data.description:
The Kennedy Center board is set to vote Tuesday on whether to immediately close the institution’s main building for renovations, as a court battle over renewed attempts to add President Trump’s name to the facility persists.

Officials have warned that the performing arts center faces “certain fiscal collapse within weeks” if it is unable to publicly recognize Trump’s fundraising role, according to a copy of a draft resolution contained in court filings.

“The Board understand that without such appropriate recognition it is unlikely that President Trump will provide the fundamental oversight of the renovation of the main building and lead the fiscal rescue of the Center,” the resolution states.

The document describes the Kennedy Center as on the brink of bankruptcy, weeks away from being unable to meet payroll or routine maintenance contracts. A second draft resolution asserts the main building is “unsafe for continued occupancy,” citing a recent water leak that caused the Grand Foyer ceiling to partially collapse.

The resolutions also position Trump’s fundraising skills as the lone hope to keep the institution afloat, with one presenting 10 different options for how the president’s name could be etched onto the building.  

“The Board seeks to provide multiple options so that President Trump can be legally and appropriately recognized and acknowledged on the façade of the Kennedy Center so that he agrees to carry the burden of managing the renovation and provides the Center with a much required financial rescue,” the resolution continues.

The plans were first reported by the Washington Post, which earlier cited confidential documents showing that ticket sales and fundraising have plummeted since the board decided to inscribe Trump’s name in December.

The board of trustees, handpicked and installed by the president, is expected to vote on the two resolutions on Tuesday afternoon. A request for comment was not immediately returned.

That meeting will come just hours after U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper holds a scheduling conference in an ongoing lawsuit brought by Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex officio board member who has led the legal challenge over the Kennedy Center changes.

“Pay up or the Kennedy Center closes, & the price is Trump’s name on the building,” Norm Eisen, one of the lawyers representing Beatty, wrote Monday on social platform X. “That’s from the board’s meeting materials, one day before they vote on it.”

“An outrageous act of hostage taking,” he added.

Cooper blocked the Kennedy Center from moving forward with a prolonged closure for renovations in late May but allowed “necessary maintenance and repair work” to continue. 

He also ordered that Trump’s name be removed from the building’s facade, concluding that the board’s initial decision was unlawful because only Congress had the authority to change the name. 

The lettering was removed in June, but the board voted on a resolution in August that would again re-add his name to the facility in the form of two inscriptions.

Cooper peppered Justice Department lawyers during a hearing last month about why the board was in a rush. The Kennedy Center has agreed to hold off until at least October 8, while also claiming the building may be demolished if the roughly $257 million renovation project is not allowed to move forward.

“The Kennedy Center is in terrible trouble,” DOJ lawyers wrote in previous court filings. “The crisis is so acute that, without the Trump Administration, its people, and President Trump, the Center cannot survive, either structurally or financially.”

data.title: GLP-1-driven vitamin deficiency linked to rare brain disorder: Study
data.description:
(NewsNation) — A new study found that a rare but serious brain condition has been identified in a small number of people taking popular weight-loss drugs such as Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro and Zepbound.

Wernicke encephalopathy is a rare neurological disorder caused by a severe deficiency of vitamin B1, also known as thiamine.

Researchers identified 15 cases reported in 2023 and 2024 among people taking GLP-1 medications containing semaglutide, found in Ozempic and Wegovy, or tirzepatide, found in Mounjaro and Zepbound.

Vitamin B1 is essential for proper nerve function. Without enough of it, patients can develop confusion, problems with balance and coordination, and abnormal eye movements.

If left untreated, the condition can lead to permanent brain damage or death. Physicians consider it a medical emergency.

GLP-1 drugs can contribute to vitamin deficiencies by suppressing appetite and reducing food intake, including foods rich in vitamin B1, such as pork, fish and whole grains.

The study found that most patients who developed the condition also experienced severe vomiting, loss of appetite, poor nutrition or rapid weight loss.

While the disorder remains rare, researchers said the findings should help doctors educate patients about the risk and monitor for warning signs.

data.title: Russian drone almost hit former CIA director; may have targeted Boris Johnson
data.description:
Former CIA Director David Petraeus on Sunday was at a Ukrainian train station while a Russian drone hit a passenger train not long after a diplomatic train carried former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and other foreign officials.

The Ukrainian state railway, Ukrzaliznytsia, stated that the diplomatic train was at the border between Ukraine and Poland after exiting the station at Yahodyn. Ukraine’s Central Monitoring Group, the dispatch unit that tracks aerial threats, notified the train’s passengers and crew to evacuate.

The alert was transmitted “literally 15 minutes before” the drone hit the train, according to a translated Telegram post.

“It is quite likely that the target of this Russian drone could also have been the diplomatic train, which departed from the station earlier than planned as part of the real-time review of train schedules due to the constant threat of Russian strikes,” Ukrainian railway officials said.

Petraeus told The New York Times that he heard the drones fly over his train, leaving Ukraine after he attended a security conference in Kyiv. He heard an explosion shortly after he and other passengers evacuated the train.

“This is the act of a truly barbaric leader trying to terrorize Ukrainian civilians,” he told the Times in a phone interview.

Johnson rode with national security advisers from several European Union and NATO member states. He later wrote on the social platform X that the Ukrzaliznytsia staff and their passengers are “absolutely heroic.”

“I don’t know what warped logic drove [Russian President Vladimir] Putin to blow up a stationary Ukrainian locomotive on the Polish border this morning,” Johnson wrote. “What we can say for sure is that this is the kind of random and senseless attack Ukrainians are enduring every day –– even on civilian railways.”

The railway stated that the diplomatic train might have been the target, noting that the train left the station earlier. The country’s rail system adjusts train schedules in response to the frequent threat of Russian attacks.

Petraeus boarded a different train and safely entered Poland. He praised Ukraine’s people as being “truly unbreakable” against Russian attacks.

Russia has intensified its campaign against Ukraine’s infrastructure, including its railways and power grid, ahead of the harsh winter season. The Russian Defense Ministry said it’s targeting “railway infrastructure facilities in western Ukraine that are used to transport military cargoes from European countries,” CNN reported, citing state news agency TASS.

These attacks have been in response to Ukrainian drone strikes on Russia’s diesel refineries, including in Siberia and the city of Nizhnekamsk, a hub for several refineries.

President Trump called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to halt the attacks on these refineries, saying that it was “hurting the world.” Diesel prices have soared to $6.23 as of Monday after an average of $3.71 last year, according to AAA.

Zelensky wrote on X on Monday that Ukraine will halt these strikes if Russia agrees to any deals facilitated by European and American partners.

“If our partners are ready to ensure that Russia genuinely refrains from striking our electricity system, other energy facilities, critical infrastructure, and food supply routes, then, of course, we are ready to ensure a corresponding halt to our strikes,” he said.

data.title: States and cities sue over 'public charge' green card restrictions
data.description:
A coalition of Democratic-led states and Washington, D.C., are suing the Trump administration to block a rule that makes it harder for immigrants to obtain green cards or even enter the country if they rely on public benefits. 

The 22 states and D.C. are challenging the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) “public charge” rule, set to take effect Friday.   

The states, led by New York Attorney General Letitia James (D), argue the rule will penalize immigrants and their families for using public benefits like food stamps, Medicaid or housing vouchers to which they are legally entitled. 

“Hardworking families should not be forced to go without the support they need because they fear asking for assistance will get them deported,” James said in a statement. “This rule preys on that fear and counts on families forfeiting the food assistance, health care coverage, and other public benefits to which they are legally entitled.” 

The lawsuit argues that under the rule, immigrants would need to stop using public assistance programs to meet their basic needs or risk being denied green cards in the future. 

Noncitizens and family members would disenroll from programs, even though they are eligible, and the states argued they will lose billions of dollars in federal funding.   

They said the rule is “arbitrary and capricious” and that DHS both ignored the harmful consequences of the change and failed to adequately justify it. 

“As households forgo their legal access to benefits—such as preventative healthcare, nutritional assistance, and school lunch—public health, local economies, public education, and public safety will suffer. The Final Rule will increase the prevalence of disease, drive up the costs of medical care, and increase poverty,” the lawsuit argued. 

A separate lawsuit challenging the rule was filed by a group of local governments, led by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D).  

The Trump administration argues the rule is necessary to protect American taxpayers from subsidizing immigrants who may become dependent on public benefits. 

The law focuses only on immigrants who are lawfully present and eligible to apply for permanent residency. Undocumented immigrants are not eligible for public benefits. 

The final rule is a revival of a similar policy that the administration tried to impose during President Trump’s first term before it was met with legal challenges and later reversed by the Biden administration. 

So-called “public charge” restrictions that bar immigrants from obtaining green cards if they are likely to rely on government assistance have been part of federal immigration policy for more than 140 years, but they have long focused only on cash benefit programs. 

The Trump administration’s first attempt to change the rule broadened the types of benefits to include the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, most Medicaid benefits and certain housing programs. 

The new rule has no limits of what can be considered, saying only that DHS “will consider the receipt of any means tested public benefits.” 

For example, if a U.S. citizen child uses state-provided health insurance, that can be used against a noncitizen parent to deny them a green card. Officers could also count a child’s participation in a school’s free lunch program against their noncitizen parent’s application for citizenship. 

“The final rule puts families in the untenable position of choosing between a U.S. citizen child’s access to healthcare, and their noncitizen parent’s ability to remain in the country,” the lawsuit argued.  

The states’ suit was brought by the attorneys general of California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Nevada, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia, along with the governor of Pennsylvania. 

Alongside New York City, the local lawsuit was brought by Chicago; the City and County of San Francisco; Santa Clara County, Calif.; Seattle and King County, Wash.

data.title: Manchin endorses Collins in Maine Senate race
data.description:
Former Sen. Joe Manchin (W.Va.), a prominent centrist who left the Democratic Party at the end of his Senate career, has endorsed Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), praising her as the “soul of the Senate.”

Manchin gave his nod to Collins over Troy Jackson, her progressive challenger who supports Medicare for All and dismantling Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

“You lose the Susan Collins’s of the Senate, you’re losing the soul of the Senate—basically, a person you can talk to, who wants to do the right thing all of the time. Now, everybody says, oh, she doesn’t do this, doesn’t speak up. Susan is always in there, always in the trenches,” Manchin said during an appearance on CNBC Monday.

Manchin and Collins worked closely together on an array of bipartisan initiatives, including the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act in 2021, a massive infrastructure bill, and the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act in 2022, which established a red-flag program to counter gun violence.

“Joe is a dear friend and trusted colleague with whom I have always worked closely to solve problems and deliver results for the people of Maine and America,” Collins said in a statement. 

“From helping end government shutdowns and negotiating the Electoral Count Act to delivering COVID relief and historic investments in our nation’s infrastructure, we have shown what is possible when Republicans and Democrats work together to find common ground and get things done. I am honored to have his support,” she said.

Manchin has recoiled at the idea of supporting candidates aligned the with the Democratic Socialists of America.

He told CBS’s Margaret Brennan, the host of “Face the Nation,” last month that there’s “no way” he would support a socialist candidate.

“No way, my God, no,” Manchin said.

“Even if they have some good ideas?” Brennan asked.

“I’ll support the good ideas, but how could you support some of the crazy stuff they’re for? Have you seen their platform?” Manchin responded.

Jackson does not identify as a democratic socialist but he has received the support of Democratic socialists, just as Graham Platner, whom Jackson replaced as the Democratic nominee in Maine, did before dropping his bid for Senate.

Manchin left the Democratic Party in May of 2024 to register as an independent. 

He frequently clashed with progressive Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) over the size of former President Biden’s Build Back Better agenda and repeatedly warned Democratic colleagues that excessive spending would fuel inflation.

data.title: From 9/11 to burn pits, we must deal with long-term effects of toxic exposure
data.description:
Two days after 9/11 my buddy and I took a bus from our hometown in Clifton, N.J., and went into Manhattan. We wandered around the city and made our way south to what would later be called Ground Zero.

There were three things from that day that are seared into my memory. The first was the families of victims at the Manhattan Armory, carrying pictures of loved ones begging people to help them find their missing family and friends. The second was the smell. It was a combination of smoke, concrete, chemicals and batteries. The third was how bad it felt to breathe. I was a smoker at the time and told my buddy when we were making our way home that I felt like I just smoked a carton of cigarettes.

Years later, in Iraq, I had the ignominious duty of burning everything that was trash every single night. We burned everything to the point that it made zero sense. I was told that we didn’t want our trash to be sifted through by the enemy, so we had to burn everything. Plastic bottles, computers, batteries, paper, and all trash. When you dared ask if it was necessary or safe, you got chewed out.

In 2011, I was at the VA in San Diego to ask about a bump in my throat. The doctors found a lump on my thyroid. I asked if it had anything to do with my exposure to burn pits. They laughed at me and said no.

A couple of years later, the lump had doubled in size and had to be removed, along with half my thyroid. They had to conduct a sleep test before I could do surgery and found I had sleep apnea. I asked again if this and the growth had anything to do with exposure and was told no.

Around the same time, the brave men and women who worked around the clock at Ground Zero started coming down with similar yet more severe symptoms. They developed respiratory issues such as coughs, wheezing, shortness of breath and asthma. They would have sinus issues and reflux from their airways into the lungs. And some got cancer. Respiratory, blood, and lymph node cancers became prevalent.

Twenty-five years since the terror attacks on the U.S., and 25 years into what we labeled a “war on terror,” we have to come to terms with the fact that long term care for both 9/11 responders and Global War on Terrorism veterans is way more complex that what we thought it would be. We also knew but chose to ignore the fact that exposure would lead to long term effects.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani made news when he said that city officials at the time knew the air quality was bad but misled people by claiming it was safe. Of course, in the world we live in people couldn’t understand why he decided to come out and talk about this, calling it some type of conspiracy theory.

There is no conspiracy. The federal, state and local authorities knew there was asbestos, chemicals and toxins in the air. They said it was safe, based on regulations at the time. But they didn’t or wouldn’t factor in long term effects. It might be safe to be at Ground Zero for a day, like I was. But repeated days that went on for months? Surely, they had to know that wasn’t safe.

It was not a fair position to be in. Then-Mayor Rudy Guiliani had to get the city back to a sense of normalcy. New York isn’t just a normal run-of-the-mill city. It was and is the financial capital of the world. The clean up efforts had to happen as fast as possible.

That means there were hard decisions to be made. Yes, you had to look at the short-term needs which were very urgent. But leadership also means balancing the short-term needs with the long-term effects. And that is where the government failed us. Millions of dollars have been paid out to 9/11 responders, even though it has taken herculean efforts from advocates like Jon Stewart. And veterans are now getting help for their own exposure to burn pits, thanks to the PACT Act.

Despite this, there is still work to be done. Long term exposure is complex and we still don’t know how bad things will get. Countless more are starting to get symptoms as they get older. We know this because the same thing happened to Vietnam veterans when they were exposed to Agent Orange or Gulf War veterans when they had to breathe in smoke from oil well fires set by Saddam Hussein. The facts show this will be an ongoing issue. Last year, over 10,000 people were diagnosed with 9/11-related cancers.

Mamdani’s release of documents about air quality was needed. We must always look out for the long-term effects even when confronted with an urgent situation. And prepare for the long-term effects, including the financial needs of those who need help. We owe it to them to seek out the truth and advocate for their continued care, no matter the cost.

Joslin Joseph is a recipient of the Military Reporters and Editors award for Best Commentary-Opinion. A graduate of Harvard and Ohio State, he is a Marine veteran who served in Iraq. He currently lives in Anaheim, Calif.

data.title: Yankee Stadium listed in Legionnaires cluster: Officials
data.description:
NEW YORK CITY (WPIX) —  A cooling tower at Yankee Stadium is among 10 towers that tested positive for Legionella bacteria on Sunday as officials investigate an outbreak in the South Bronx.

The New York City Department of Health said all cooling towers that tested positive for Legionella have been ordered to be cleaned and disinfected by Monday.

Officials said polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing can detect the presence of Legionella but cannot show whether the bacteria are alive and does not confirm a cooling tower as the source of exposure. They also reiterated that only live Legionella can cause illness.

Officials urged anyone who lives, works or has visited the affected area since late August and develops flu‑like symptoms to contact a health care provider immediately.

They also said it is safe to shower, drink tap water and use air conditioners in the affected ZIP codes. Officials noted there is no additional risk from being inside any of the 10 buildings.

There will be an in-person town hall for residents to sit down with public health officials on Tuesday at 6 p.m at Metropolitan College in the Bronx.

One person has died in connection with the South Bronx outbreak, and five cases have been confirmed, according to officials.

On the Upper East Side, a Legionnaires’ cluster claimed nine lives and led to more than 90 confirmed cases, with the outbreak first reported at the beginning of July.

Yankee Stadium released the following statement on Sunday night:

In 2024, the Yankees installed new, state-of-the-art, high-efficiency chiller towers at Yankee Stadium, which have undergone water quality and bacteriological indicator testing on a weekly basis over the last three years.

In accordance with DOH regulations, Yankee Stadium provides these results to the DOH on a monthly basis. In the most recent monthly testing on Aug. 20, which was provided to the Department of Health, results were negative for Legionella bacteria. Subsequent to that test, weekly water quality and bacteriological indicator testing was performed on Aug. 26, Sept. 2 and Sept. 9.

Due to the recent community cluster of Legionella bacteria in the Melrose and Morrisania areas of the Bronx (zip codes 10451 and 10456) last week, the NYC Dept. of Health conducted 24 PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) tests of cooling towers in the area, including one at Yankee Stadium on Sept. 11. Yankee Stadium tested positive for trace amounts of Legionella bacteria and was one of 10 cooling towers in the Bronx that tested positive.

A PCR test, which is different from the independent monthly testing Yankee Stadium regularly undertakes, can detect the presence of Legionella bacteria DNA but cannot determine whether the bacteria are alive or dead and does not confirm that a cooling tower is the source of exposure. Only live Legionella bacteria can cause illness.

No current cases have been associated with Yankee Stadium. Additionally, the New York City Department of Health has not at any point this month asked us to postpone our games.

The Health Department is now conducting culture testing to determine whether live Legionella bacteria were present when the samples were collected. Culture results can take up to two weeks.

To reduce the risk of ongoing exposure while culture testing continues, the Health Department mandated that all cooling towers with a positive PCR result conduct a full hyperhalogenation, including draining, cleaning, and disinfection.

Immediate action was taken, and this was completed at Yankee Stadium earlier this morning (Sunday).

To exercise an abundance of caution, those who currently live, work or have visited the two ZIP codes since late August and are experiencing flu-like symptoms, such as fever, cough, or difficulty breathing, should contact a healthcare provider immediately.

Please note that Legionnaires’ disease is not contagious and can be treated with antibiotics when caught early.

data.title: Donald Trump is right: 'Whoever wins AI, wins' — no pause!
data.description:
As a variety of pundits from across the political spectrum make clear they desperately want to regulate AI, President Trump is holding the line. He announced the following yesterday:  

 “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades! The Trump Administration has stopped AI ‘people’ from doing bad, or potentially bad, ‘things,’ like Dario (Anthropic!), who is now pretending to be a ‘perfect little angel’ – and we will continue to do so! We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies! There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS! We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so. Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers, BEWARE! Thank you for your attention to this matter! President DONALD J. TRUMP”  

Vice President Vance echoed those comments. 

On the other side, Democrats strongly believe more regulation is necessary — even existential. Here was Sen. Jon Ossoff.

That ex-Anthropic whistleblower he mentioned, Jacob Coxon, is joining forces with Bernie Sanders, and also Steve Bannon apparently. They will appear together at an ostensibly “pro human” AI event.  

And already, there are huge efforts underway to guilt Trump into going along. I saw reports yesterday that advisers in the White House are urging Trump to address the nation and promise some new wave of AI legislation. OpenAI’s Sam Altman is making his appeal based on Trump’s love of winning prizes, and says if Trump and Xi Jinping come together to safeguard AI, they should win the Nobel Peace Prize.  

Now this all sounds good in theory. Who is against sensible regulation to make sure AI superintelligence doesn’t pose a threat to humanity?  

In theory, no one. But when we get more specific than that, what Anthropic is asking for doesn’t really make sense: i.e., putting in limitations so these so-called frontier models have to advance slowly. A regulation to prevent swift advancement actually benefits whichever company is already winning, by making it impossible for some other AI competitor to catch up. That’s not fair — it’s regulatory capture, and it’s something that happens all the time, despite Rahm Emanuel’s contention that he’s unfamiliar with CEOs begging for regulation.  

The dominant market player is often interested in regulation! It happens all the time! They want to kneecap their competitors and remain in their position of dominance! That’s what matters most to Anthropic, believe you me.  

So what’s the remedy? Well, as former FTC commissioner Lina Khan points out, there are already laws on the books to punish companies from releasing defective products out onto the market. I never ever ever ever ever agree with Lina Khan, and I think she has a broad conception of consumer harm that ends up punishing large companies for making products that their consumers actually do want. But in this case she’s raising a valid point: Harm to the consumer is already the point of antitrust law, and if any AI company is flouting that, there can already be consequences. It’s perfectly fine to enforce that.  

And that’s basically what Trump was saying: Millions of Americans chose Trump to be their president in this moment because they trust his judgment. He seems to understand that we need to let AI companies compete with one another to offer useful new models, and that any company that does something hostile or intrinsically evil can face the necessary consequences. So based on that, I would recommend the AI doomers should chill out.  

Robby Soave is co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising” and a senior editor for Reason Magazine. This column is an edited transcription of his daily commentary.

data.title: Top Oversight Democrat wants answers on Russian oligarch's role in Trump Jr.'s wedding
data.description:
Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), the ranking member on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, pressed for answers on a Russian oligarch’s reported role in a wedding for one of President Trump’s sons.

According to a report published Monday by ProPublica, Donald Trump Jr.’s wedding in May received funding from Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev, who is linked to Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The outlet reported that the oligarch paid for Trump Jr.’s wedding expenses in the hundreds of thousands of dollars, citing records and three sources with knowledge of the event. For the president’s son’s big event, ProPublica reported, Kremlev helped rent an island and put up the money for a fireworks show.

“Why did a Russian oligarch close to Putin fund Trump Jr.’s wedding in the Bahamas?” Garcia said in a Monday morning post on the social platform X, responding to the report.

“Umar Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on the President’s son. What did he get in return? We need answers,” he added.

Last December, Trump Jr. said that he was engaged at the White House holiday party in front of family, friends and guests. The president’s son called his engagement to Bettina Anderson, a Palm Beach, Fla., socialite, a “big win” for the end of 2025.

Trump Jr.’s wife, who now goes by Bettina Trump, clapped back at the ProPublica report in an Instagram post on Monday, saying that she and her husband “got married privately on” May 22, “surrounded ONLY by our family.”

“Our dear friend Umar very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding. It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful,” she added later.

The Hill has reached out to Kremlev for comment.
